Postmortem: Object Storage Elevated Latency and Partial Unavailability
Incident ID: INC-3305 | Basalt Cloud Platform | Date: Jan 25
Authors: Petra Novakova, Hiroshi Sato

Summary
Between 04:10 and 06:55 UTC, the object storage service experienced elevated write latency (p99 over 8 seconds, versus a normal p99 of 200ms) in the eu-west region only. Approximately 3% of write requests in eu-west failed outright during the worst 20 minutes (04:40-05:00).

Timeline
- 04:10 - Write latency begins climbing in eu-west following a routine capacity rebalance that started at 04:05.
- 04:18 - Automated alert fires for elevated p99 latency; on-call Hiroshi Sato acknowledges.
- 04:25 - Hiroshi's initial hypothesis: the rebalance itself is the cause, based on timing.
- 04:40 - Write failures begin as a subset of storage nodes become unresponsive under the rebalance load.
- 04:52 - Hiroshi escalates to Petra Novakova.
- 05:05 - Petra identifies that the rebalance job's concurrency setting was left at a testing-environment value (50 parallel moves) instead of the production value (10), due to a configuration file that wasn't updated when the rebalance tool was promoted to production two weeks earlier.
- 05:20 - Rebalance job is paused; concurrency reset to 10.
- 05:35 - Write failures stop; latency begins recovering.
- 06:55 - p99 latency returns to baseline.

Root cause
A configuration file for the rebalance tool retained a testing-environment concurrency value after promotion to production, causing 5x the intended number of parallel data moves and overwhelming a subset of storage nodes.

Scope
Only eu-west was affected; us-east and ap-southeast regions run independent rebalance schedules and were not touched by this job. No data loss occurred - failed writes were client-side failures (the client received an error and could retry), not partial or corrupted writes accepted by the service.

Customer impact
An estimated 40 customers in eu-west experienced at least one failed write during the 20-minute worst window. Basalt's status page was updated at 04:50, twenty minutes after the alert fired, which the team flagged as slower than the 10-minute target in the incident-communication policy.

Action items
1. Add a config-drift check comparing production values against the testing template after every promotion - owner: Petra, due Feb 8.
2. Reduce status-page update SLA breach risk by adding a checklist reminder to the on-call runbook - owner: Hiroshi, due Feb 1.
3. Audit all other tools promoted in the last quarter for similar leftover testing configuration - owner: Petra, due Feb 15.

What went well
Once identified, the fix (pausing the job and resetting concurrency) took under 15 minutes to resolve the immediate write failures.

Monthly Program Report - Cascadia Freight Fleet Telematics Rollout
Month: February | Sponsor: Tariq Hassan | Program Lead: Beatriz Souza

Executive summary
The telematics hardware rollout across Cascadia's 1,200-truck fleet is 65% complete (780 trucks), on pace for the planned April 30 completion.

Installation progress
- Pacific region: 310 of 320 trucks complete (97%)
- Mountain region: 280 of 350 trucks complete (80%)
- Central region: 190 of 530 trucks complete (36%) - behind pace due to a parts shortage described below

Parts shortage
The GPS antenna model specified for this rollout has a 6-week backorder from the manufacturer, first reported Jan 15. Pacific and Mountain regions had already stocked enough units before the shortage hit; Central region had not, which explains its lower completion rate. A substitute antenna model has been qualified as of Feb 20 and Central region installations resume at full pace this week.

Budget
Approved budget: $3.6M. Spend to date: $2.1M. The parts shortage has not increased per-unit cost - the substitute antenna is priced the same as the original - but it has pushed roughly $400K of planned February spend into March as installations slipped.

Driver feedback
A survey of 150 drivers with the new system installed found 82% reported the new fuel-efficiency coaching feature 'somewhat' or 'very' useful. The remaining 18% cited the in-cab alert sound as too frequent; a software update reducing alert frequency ships March 5.

Safety metrics
Hard-braking events per 1,000 miles dropped 22% fleet-wide among trucks with telematics installed for at least 30 days, compared to a control group of not-yet-installed trucks over the same period.

Risks
1. (Medium) If the substitute antenna reveals any unforeseen compatibility issue at scale, Central region could fall further behind; the team is monitoring the first 50 substitute installations closely before scaling up.
2. (Low) Driver survey response rate was only 12.5% (150 of 1,200); results should be treated as directional, not conclusive, until a larger sample is collected at the 90-day mark.

Next steps
Beatriz to report Central region's substitute-antenna install rate weekly through March. Tariq to review the shifted March budget with Finance.

Vendor note
The antenna manufacturer has confirmed the original model's backorder will clear by late March, but the team plans to continue with the substitute model for the remainder of the rollout regardless, since qualifying a second supplier reduces future single-vendor risk. This decision was made jointly by Beatriz and Tariq after the Feb 20 qualification results came back clean.

Vendor Evaluation Call - Driftwood Airlines Crew Scheduling
Rep: Dmitri Volkov | Feb 25

Dmitri: Thanks for the time. Last we spoke you were also considering building this in-house. Where does that stand?

Contact (Julia Castellano, VP Operations, Driftwood Airlines): We got a rough estimate from our engineering team - 14 months and roughly $1.8M fully loaded, mostly because crew-scheduling rules for airlines are genuinely complex with FAA rest-time rules.

Dmitri: How does that compare to what you're seeing from vendors like us?

Julia: Your quote is $420,000/year, and a competitor, a company called Skyframe Systems, quoted $380,000/year. Both are obviously cheaper than building it ourselves over any reasonable timeframe, so build-vs-buy isn't really the live question anymore. It's you versus Skyframe.

Dmitri: Understood. Can I ask what's driving the gap toward Skyframe on price?

Julia: Skyframe's price is lower, but they've never implemented for an airline our size - their biggest customer is a regional carrier with 40 aircraft, we have 210. You've done three airlines our size or larger, which matters more to us than the $40,000/year difference.

Dmitri: That's helpful context. Is there anything Skyframe offers that we don't, that's swaying things their way?

Julia: Not that I've seen. If anything, our ops team found their demo less polished. I want to be honest with you though - our CFO looks at the raw number first, so you may need to help me build the case for the experience premium being worth $40K/year.

Dmitri: Understood, I can put together a one-pager quantifying implementation risk for a carrier our size versus Skyframe's track record. Would a reference call with one of our similar-sized airline customers help?

Julia: Yes, that would help a lot with the CFO conversation specifically.

Dmitri: I'll set that up this week. To confirm - building in-house is off the table at this point?

Julia: Correct, off the table. Timeline alone rules it out even before cost - 14 months is too slow regardless of price.

Dmitri: One more thing - what's your internal timeline for a decision, so I know how to pace the reference call and one-pager?

Julia: We'd like to decide by the end of March, ideally, so our new scheduling process is live well before next winter's peak season.

Action items: Dmitri to arrange a reference call with a comparable airline customer by March 3. Dmitri to send a one-pager on implementation risk at scale.

Kestrel Media Platform - Changelog v11.0 through v11.3

v11.0 (Mar 10)
- New: Multi-author collaboration on drafts (up to 5 simultaneous editors, up from 1).
- New: Analytics dashboard adds a 'read completion rate' metric alongside existing pageviews.
- Breaking: The /v1/articles endpoint's author field (a single string) is replaced by an authors array. Integrations reading the old author field will get an empty value, not an error - this is a silent breaking change with no exceptions.

v11.1 (Mar 24)
- Fixed: Read-completion-rate metric undercounted for articles with embedded video, since video-heavy scroll behavior wasn't accounted for; now corrected.
- New: Draft version history now retains 90 days of history, up from 30 days, for all tiers including Free.

v11.2 (Apr 7)
- New: Scheduled publishing can now target a specific timezone per article, instead of always using account-default timezone.
- Fixed: Multi-author collaboration occasionally showed a stale cursor position for the second editor; now syncs in real time.

v11.3 (Apr 21)
- Breaking: Free tier's draft version history retention is reduced back to 30 days (the 90-day retention introduced in v11.1 is now Pro-tier and above only). Free-tier drafts older than 30 days as of this release are not retroactively deleted, but new drafts follow the 30-day limit.
- New: Multi-author collaboration limit raised from 5 to 10 simultaneous editors for Enterprise tier only; other tiers remain at 5.
- Deprecated: The legacy /v1/articles author string field entirely stops being populated (previously it silently returned empty; now it's removed from the response object). Use authors.

Known issues (as of v11.3)
- A handful of Enterprise customers report the 10-editor collaboration limit isn't yet reflected in their account settings UI, though it works correctly when tested directly; a UI fix is planned for v11.4.

Migration guide
Any integration still reading the author string field must migrate to authors - this became silently empty in v11.0 and is fully removed as of v11.3. Free-tier customers relying on 90-day draft history should note the reduction back to 30 days in v11.3, though nothing already older than 30 days was deleted retroactively.

Support notes
Most v11.0 migration tickets were about the author field change; support reports the silent-empty behavior caused more confusion than a hard error would have, since integrations didn't immediately notice anything was wrong. Support now recommends Kestrel flag silent-empty breaking changes more prominently and more loudly in future release notes going forward.
